description: 2011 March-June: An "intense round of lobbying" regionally and internationally in response to several incidents with China, including the Zone of Peace, Freedom, Friendship and Cooperation (ZOPFF/C) initiative. (Thayer, Chinese Assertiveness)

2011 March 28: AFP chief General Eduardo Oban announces that PHL military has increased air and sea patrols in the SCS and reiterated plans upgrade the Thitu/Pagasa airstrip and barracks (Thayer, Chinese Assertiveness, 80).
other_possible_cases: 2011, May: PHL military removes PRC buoys and markers from Amy Douglas Bank (Zhang, Appendix II, 12). This was in response to new construction.

description: 2011, June 30: PHL launches 4th Energy Contracting Round, offering up Area 3 and Area 4 inside the nine-dash line to exploration (Rappler, "3 PH groups bid"). Open to domestic and foreign firms.
2011, July: Philippines Navy builds new permanent structures on Flat Island (Patag 费信岛) (Laude, "Navy seabees constructing 'starshell'")

2011 July 21: Visit to Thitu/Pagasa by Philippine politicians, who sing the national anthem with Kalayaan residents. (https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-pacific-14212130; https://globalnation.inquirer.net/6601/%E2%80%98spratly-5%E2%80%99-go-swimming-in-pag-asa)
other_possible_cases: 2011, May 26: PH media reports "A Philippine government briefing paper said that “Vietnam is at the forefront of construction activities, having built the most number of additional structures at its occupied territories since 1998.”  -- mainly solar panel

description: 2011, October: Reed Bank dinghies incident. Chinese trawler was confronted by a Philippine Navy warship, and hastily released more than thirty dinghies it was then towing, which were then confiscated. (Koh, "The Philippines' Navy Challenge").
other_possible_cases: 2011, October 19: Philippines Defense Department apologises, then the Philippines Foreign Ministry says there is no need to apologise, for one of its warships "accidentally" ramming a small Chinese fishing boat. ('Manila apologises to China over South Chi

description: 2012 April: PHL Navy attempts to arrest PRC fishing militia, triggering Scarbrough Shoal standoff (Van Pham, The Use or Threat of Force, 533; Hayton, The South China Sea, 115, 160)
other_possible_cases: 2012: “In 2012, the Philippines offered China the opportunity to take their dispute over Scarborough Shoal to a number of dispute settlement mechanisms, including the International Tribunal under the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) or other international bodies, a

description: 2012, April-June: PHL makes strong public campaign against PRC actions at Scarborough Shoal, including publicizing photographs, and lobbying ASEAN for a statement on the matter. In subsequent years Manila continues to speak out strongly against the PRC's seizure of the shoal.

2012 June: Philippines opens school on Thitu/Pagasa. “China made diplomatic protests about the school opening, arguing it was a violation of its ‘indisputable sovereignty’ in the South China Sea.” (Hayton, The South China Sea, 105-106).
other_possible_cases: 2012 (late March): China and Taiwan protest Philippines's announcement that "it would build a 300-foot wharf in the Spratlys on Thitu Island" (CSIS, Countering Coercion 98)

description: 2012, July 31: PHL Dept of Energy accepts bids from domestic companies on Area 3 and Area 4 which lie within the nine-dash line. (Rappler, “3 PH groups bid") Given to domestic companies, so declarative and administrative, rather than demonstrative and diplomatic. Action paused from Arbitration case onwards.
2012 September: South China Sea officially named “West Philippine Sea” in the Philippines. (Hayton, The South China Sea, 165)
2013 January 22: PHL serves PRC with notice of its launching of an arbitration case under Annex 287 of the UNCLOS
other_possible_cases: 2013 May: Philippine naval vessel fires at Taiwanese fishing boat, killing one crew member [occurred in disputed EEZ, closer to Philippines, may or may not have been directly in the SCS]. (Taiwan Demands Philippine Apology for Fisherman's Killing:, https:

description: 2013, November 12: Second Thomas Shoal building supply mission brings “roofing and good lumber for repairs” to the ship’s hull, which had been damaged during Typhoon Haiyan, consolidating the rusting hulk BRP Sierra Madre where a small detachment of marines are stationed (CSIS 2017, 181). On March 9, 2014 another mission to Second Thomas Shoal brings, in words of PHL officials quoted in the media, "supplies and equipment for repair" and materials for "repairs inside the ship to keep it from disintegrating,” (CSIS 2017, 184-185). Chinese Coast Guard prevents Philippine ships from reaching the shoal, but according to PHL Navy officials later in the year it began transporting  “light construction materials” including “cement, settle, cabling, and welding equipment.” Construction proceeds quietly through 2015 (CSIS 2017, 197-199).
other_possible_cases: 2013, August: NYT facilitated to go to Second Thomas Shoal. Arguably part of the publicity strategy that emerged the following year (and which had been used before after Mischief Reef). But actually the NYT reporter worked very hard to make the trip happe

description: 2013 May: Philippine naval vessel fires at Taiwanese fishing boat, killing one crew member  in disputed EEZ  (Taiwan Demands Philippine Apology for Fisherman's Killing:, https://search.proquest.com/docview/1349843860/fulltext/22C4042EAB854CB9PQ/1?accountid=11243); Taiwan Ends Sanctions Against Philippines Over Shooting Death, https://search.proquest.com/docview/1418898053?accountid=11243; Van Pham, The Use or Threat of Force, 534).

2014, February 4: Rhetorical escalation as Philippines President Aquino likens China’s behavior in the South China Sea to Germany in Czechoslovakia in 1938 (Bradsher, "Philippine Leader Sounds Alarm").
other_possible_cases: 2014 April: Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) finalized, “allows for the increased presence of U.S. military forces, ships, aircraft, and equipment in the Philippines on a nonpermanent basis and greater U.S. access to Philippine military bases

description: 2014, March 14: Manila refers to Second Thomas Shoal it for the first time as a “permanent Philippine Government installation.” Two days earlier, the United States had affirmed that Philippine efforts to preserve its crumbling position on the reef were maintaining the “status quo.” (Chubb, "Chinese Nationalism and the Gray Zone," 70).
other_possible_cases: 2014, May 9: 5th Energy Contracting Round (PECR 5) announced. Includes disputed Area 7 between Reed Bank SC72 and nine-dash line. (Official Gazette, "DOE opens 5th Philippine energy contracting round for coal and petroleum exploration")

description: 2014, March 29: Interational media trips to Second Thomas Shoal. With US, PHL and PRC air surveillance above, a Philippine vessel carrying journalists outmaneuvers Chinese ships, resupplying Philippine occupants of the Second Thomas Shoal; reporters were invited on the ship by the Philippine government (de Castro & Ng, "Philippine ship dodges China blockade"; CSIS 2017, 189-195). Another journalists' trip to the shoal is organized in late April, arriving in early May (CSIS 2017, 196).
2014 May: PHL detains 11 Chinese fishermen for catching endangered sea turtles in disputed waters at Half Moon Shoal, Spratlys. Nine are charged. (Zhang and Bateman, Fishing Militia, 298-299)
2014 May-June: The Philippines publishes photos of alleged Chinese island building in the South China Sea Johnson South, Gaven and Cuarteron Reefs (Diola, "IN PHOTOS: China's reclamation").

2015 April: Largest ever Balikatan joint military exercises, with 11,000 soldiers and sailors, reportedly more than twice the number in the 2014 exercise  (Harkins, "The new look"). Assuming it did not take place in the disputed area.

1971 May: South Vietnam conducts surveys in Paracel Islands (NSZGSZHS 212; Pedrozo, China versus Vietnam). Jones mentions surveys at Triton and Duncan (Jones, Power Politics in Asia’s Contested Waters, 212).

1973 (January 29, May 7 & 23, August 8 & 14) South Vietnam deploys ships to both Paracels and Spratlys, including Philippines-occupied Thitu (中业岛), Nanyue (南钥岛), and North (北子岛)  to conduct reconaissance and survey activities (NSZGSZHS 119, 212, 221).

1973 July: South Vietnam grants first oil concessions to foreign firms. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 45; NSZGSZHS 213; Hayton, The South China Sea, 71; Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, 19). Eight contracts were awarded.
1973 July 12:  South Vietnamese destroyers bring personnel and materials to support construction/long-term occupation on Namyit Island (鸿庥). (NSZGSZHS 119, 221). AMTI says it was 1974.
1973 Fall: South Vietnamese government publishes map, including the Paracels in South Vietnam's territory (NSZGSZHS 213). Frst time? Needs checking.

1973 September: South Vietnam formally annexes 10 islands in the Spratly Islands to protect oil exploration, deploying hundreds of troops on Namyit Island. (Hayton, The South China Sea, 71). NSZGSZHS indicates late 1973 or January 1974, and maybe 11 features? (NSZGSZHS 17, 119).

1973, November: South Vietnam rams Chinese fishing boat, detains crew, and forces them to confess that the Paracels belong to Vietnam. (盘点中国历次反击战：人民日报发完社论后开打 http://www.peacehall.com/news/gb/z_special/2012/05/201205130534.shtml -- see also Benson, "South China Sea").

1974 January 18: South Vietnamese foreign minister tells the United Nations that the Paracel and Spratly Islands are Vietnamese territory. The language employed is  similar to modern Chinese rhetoric on the South China Sea. Claimed sovereignty to the UN again in March. (不可分割的一部分，这一事实是明显的, 不可否认的) (NSZGSZHS 214). On January 29 the South Vietnamese military command releases revised injuries and death count from the battle that month: in the two days battle, one ship was sunk and three damaged (unclear which side this is referring to).
diminished_notes: 1974: Vietnam loses control of the Paracel Islands. Previously listed occupations of features in the Paracel Islands listed as ending in 1974, so be sure not to double count.
other_possible_cases: 1974 January 15-19: Battle of the Parcel Islands. The consensus of non-Chinese sources seems to be that China *started* the conflict, but Vietnam definately used military force, so..? (NSZGSZHS 18-19, 21-34, 208-225; Garver, China's push; Hayton, The South China Sea, 73; Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 46). I don't think this counts as an intensification of assertiveness - it's certainly a diminishment as they ceased to occupy these disputed features.

description: 1974 January 30 to February 8, 17-20: South Vietnam occupies various features in the Spratly Islands. Occupies or strengthens presence on Nanwei, Nanzi, Dunqian, Jinghong, and erects a sovereignty marker on Anbo. Also starts construction. Reports claim between 4-7 features. (NSZGSZHS 20, 119-120, 222-224; Chen Jie PhD, p.151; AMTI). March 30: South Vietnam publishes the names of the 5 islands it is occupying in the Spratly Islands (or at least 5 new ones?):  Nanwei (南威岛), Skylark/Yunque [云雀] (判敦谦沙洲), Shuangzixi [双子西] (南子岛), Shengcun [生存] (景宏), and Nanxie [南歇] (鸿庥岛) (NSZGSZHS 115-124).

1974 February: Spike in rhetorical assertions of sovereignty over the Paracel and Spratly Islands by South Vietnam, including expressions of willingness to use force to gain complete control over the island groups. (NSZGSZHS 216-217).

1974: Major hydrocarbon developments launched by South Vietnam. First geophysical surveys of Phu Khanh Basin and Nam Con Son Basin (no PetroVietnam data) (H. Luong Lien, The Economics of Petroleum 1998 Exploraiton, 6.26). In August first wildcat wells (oil) drilled in Nam Con Son Basin (Hong 1, Block 12E). (H. Luong Lien, The Economics of Petroleum 1998 Exploraiton, 6.6-6.7) Pecten discovers first oil and gas in Nam Con Son Basin (Dua 1, Block 12E). (H. Luong Lien, The Economics of Petroleum 1998 Exploraiton, 6.17)

1975, early: Southwest Cay incident, in which South Vietnamese troops occupy Philippine-held Southwest Cay while its garrison was at a party on neighbouring Northwest Cay. A few months later Southwest Cay becomes the first target of North Vietnamese troops when they arrive (Hayton, South China Sea, 101-102).
other_possible_cases: 1975 April 29: Vietnam occupies Anbo Shoal? AMTI says Vietnam occupied Anbo in 1974, Rosenberg says 1975 or 1979 http://www.southchinasea.org/2011/08/19/digital-gazetteer-of-the-spratly-islands/, Dzurek says sometime after 1978, and NSZGSZHS says 1975 April 29 on page 204 (using 侵驻) and says 1973 on page 245 (using 侵占). Not a big problem for us, because it's either counted under the 1975 occupations or the 1978 occupations.

description: 1975 February 14: South Vietnam publishes a white paper, reaffirming its clam to sovereignty over the Spratly Islands (NSZGSZHS 120; Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 46 dates this White Paper to April 1975).

1975 April-May: Vietnam takes control of South Vietnamese possessions in the Spratly Islands. NSZGSZHS says various points in April, Garver says April, Do Thanh Hai says May, a different reference book says May, and Dzurek says April. (NSZGSZHS 115-124, 203-207; Garver; NSZGSZHS 115-124; other reference book?; Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, 19).

1975 May 5-6: “the delegation of the Provisional Revolutionary Government in South Vietnam to the Colombo Meteorological Conference requested the World Meteorological Organization to continue to recognise Vietnam’s meteorological station, No.48.860, on the Hoang Sa Islands and opposed China’s registration for its station there.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 48).

1975 August: Victorious North Vietnam issues resolution outlining guidelines for oil and gas exploration throughout the country. "It identified the continental shelf off the southern coast and the Tonkin Gulf in the South China Sea as priority exploration areas" (ICG, Oil in Troubled Waters, 11).

1975 September 25: “After reunification, Hanoi departed from its customary passive position, openly asserting Vietnam’s sovereignty over the Paracel and Spratly archipelagos. In an official meeting on 25 September 1975, Vietnamese party chief Le Duan officially raised the status of the Paracel and Spratly Islands with Chinese Vice Premier Deng Xiaoping.” Followed up with a forceful note in November. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 48).
1975-1976: Vietnam occupies another 7 islands for a total of 13 (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 48; NSZGSZHS 47-48).
1975, presumably late in the year: Vietnam builds airstrip on Spratly Island (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 48; NSZGSZHS 47-48).
1976: Vietnamese forces on Southwest Cay fire on nearby Philippine aircraft (Van Pham, "Use or Threat of Force," 525).

1977 May 12: Vietnam unilaterally issues “Statement on the Territorial Sea, Contiguous Zone, Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental Shelf.” Followed up in 1982. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 52; Nansha, "Nanhai Zhudao").

1978 March-April: Vietnam occupies multiple features in the Spratly Islands. Features include Shuanghuang Shoal/Bank (双黄沙洲), Ranqing Shoal/Bank (染青沙洲), Nailuo Reef (奈罗礁), Zhong Reef (中礁). Vietnam also entered and planted flags at Zhubi (渚碧) Reef, Changxian Reef (长线礁). Vietnam also entered two unnamed [redacted??] islands (Vietnamese names provided: Yuchuan Island [渔船岛] and Pangrong Island [潘荣岛], with a sovereignty marked erected on Yuchuan). (NSZGSZHS 121-122; 203-207).

1978, April 26: Vietnam Central TV broadcasts first Spratly documentary, indicating that its maritime consciousness struggle is already in progress. The documentary emphasizes how "these islands belong to Vietnam, Vietnamese people's footprints appeared long ago in these remote islands". (Zhang, NSQDDSJ, 63).
1978: first geophysical survey of Song Hong Basin (no PetroVietnam data). (Lien, "The Economics of Petroleum," 6.27).

1979 April 10: Vietnam deployed 3 ships of soldiers to conduct reconaissance within 500 meters of [Chinese possessions in?] the Paracel Islands, allegedly provoking Chinese forces by shooting. Apparently not the only recent provocation of this nature, and these provoctions are taking place amid Sino-Vietnamese negotiations (NSZGSZHS 36-38; Garver, "China's push")
1980, Feb: Vietnam holds military exercises in Spratlys (Nansha, "Nanhai Zhudao")

1980 July: Vietnam and the Soviet Union sign an agreement on the cooperative exploration and mining of oil and natural gas in Vietnam's continental shelf (NSZGSZHS 40; Zhang Liangfu NSQDDSJ, 88; Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, 18) In 1985 the Soivet Union and Vietnam sign a long term oil exploration and production plan, part of a broader plan to expand Vietnam's energy production (NSZGSHS 352-355). Partnerships with USSR were likely inherited by Russia.
1981: energy development intensifies with first magnetic and gravity surveys of Nam con Son Basin and Song Hong Basins (Lien, "The Economics of Petroleum," 6.28).
1982, February: Vietnamese ships detain Guangzhou trawlers fishing in the Paracels. China retaliated by capturing a Vietnamese vessel (Garver 1992, 1008; Fisheries Yearbook 2000, 269).

1982 June: Vietnamese navy second in command (越南海军一副司令) inspects the Spratly Islands (NSZGSZHS 122). These sorts of visits continue regularly, one or two visits every few years, into the early 1990s, at least to 1993, and then again in 2003.
1982 November 12: Vietnamese government publishes statement on territorial seas baseline (NSZGSZHS 41, 122; Zhang Liangfu NSQDDSJ 93-94; Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 52).
1983 November 12: Vietnam and the Soviet Union collaborate to use Ilyushin-18 (伊尔-18型) aircraft to atmospheric survey in the Spratly Islands (NSZGSZHS 122).

1987: Occupation of numerous features. In February/April, depending on source, Vietnam occupies Barque Canada Reef (Bo Jiao) (NSZGSZHS 42, 123, 203-207; Garver; AMTI). Between December 1987 and March 1988: Vietnam successively occupies features in the Spratly Islands, including East Reef, West Reef, Discovery Great (Daxian) Reef, Alison (Liumen) Reef, Cornwallis South (Nanhua) Reef, Pigeon (Wumie) Reef, Ladd (Riji) Reef, Bolan (Petley) Reef, and on Bisheng (Pearson) Reef, Gaven (Nan) Reef, Subi (Zhubi) Reef, and Jieri Reef planted flags and erected markers (NSZGSZHS 121, 203-207, 245-248; Fravel; Thu Thiem)

1987 (onward): Offering of offshore oil concessions to foreign companies, including in disputed areas. "After the Foreign Investment Law was promulgated at the end of 1987, the government opened up offshore areas for petroleum exploration to foreign companies." The following year Vietnam published its expansive oil and gas blocks map covering areas claimed by all other claimants. (VN MOFA spokesman statement, April 20, 1994, reprinted in Zhang Liangfu NSQDDSJ 253).

1988 February 20: Vietnamese foreign ministry spokesperson demands that Chinese ships investigating (考察) and patrolling the Spratly Islands leave or "accept full responsibility for the consequences" (撤离并扬言要中国对"所引起一切后果承担全部责任"). (NSZGSZHS 45)
diminished_notes: 1988 (after South Johnson skirmish): Overall, Vietnam softens rhetoric toward China and calls for talks. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 51, 68).
other_possible_cases: 1988 February 18: Cuarteron Reef incident (Garver; Fravel; Thu Thiem). I am a little unclear of what exactly happened here, since I didn't see it in any of my research, but it looks like you ran across it in several sources? After looking at What Garver said, it just seems to be part of Vietnam's increased presence. Yes, it would be covered in the existing cases of intensification.

description: 1988: Mobilization of population before and after South Johnson Reef skirmish. the whole country surging with anti-China waves" (在全国上下掀起反华浪潮), mobilizing the masses of every sphere to assist Vietnam's operations in the Spratlys (NSZGSZHS 46). Do Thanh Hai notes that after China takes Cuarteron Reef, Vietnam begins internal mobilization of groups like the Youth Union and Vietnam Lawyer’s Association (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 50).
other_possible_cases: 1988 (around March?): Vietnam has recently deployed numerous ships to the maritime space of the Spratly Islands.  The Vietnamese air force has also stepped up operations. (NSZGSZHS 46; Garver) I'd say not an act of intensified assertiveness, given what the PRC had just done. If PRC had done that earlier, I think VN would very likely have at least done this in respones.

description: 1988 March-April on: major international PR campaign, with Vietnam making strong efforts to convince the United Nations that the Spratly and Paracel islands belong to Vietnam and that China provoked the skirmish on Johnson South Reef (NSZGSZHS 54-55, 56-59). UN efforts are aided by Cambodia (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 50-51)
other_possible_cases: 1988 March 14: South Johnson Reef skirmish. Chinese say Vietnamese opened fire first, Vietnamese say Chinese opened fire first. As of March 16, there was no further armed conflict since that incident on the 14th. Assuming this counts for force for Vietnam even if they did not *start* it? (NSZGSZHS 46; Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 50-51). VN used force here but I don't think it constituted an intensification of its assertiveness. The PRC occupying reefs in the Spratlys by force was an entirely new situation, and one in which we would have expected VN to respond this way in any earlier year too.

description: 1988 March-May: post-skirmish occupations and construction by Vietnam in the Spratly Islands. PLA tells reporters that after the 3-14 incident, Vietnam occupied Qiong Reef (琼) and Guihan Reef (鬼喊). AMTI confirms that these two reefs were indeed occupied in 1988. PLA alleges that Vietnam has built up forces on the newly occupied (1988) islands and reefs, including Daxian (大现), Nanhua  (南华), Liumen  (六门), Wumie (无乜), Riji (日积), and Dong Reef (东) (NSZGSZHS 54-55).

1988 April - June: Vietnamese moves to shore up its existing positions in Spratly Islands after the Johnson South Reef skirmish. In April thirty Vietnamese ships are deployed to Spratly Islands to block further Chinese expansion. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 51). May: Vietnam's Defense Minister Le Duc Anh visits the Spratlys to inspect troops and vow to defend Spratly Islands, and Vietnamese Navy conducts live-fire exercises. (Wen Hui Bao, quote Garver 2009; Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 51).
1988 June: Vietnam sends 150 "construction workers" to Spratlys to construct barracks on one island. (Zhang Liangfu NSQDDSJ 163).

1988 onwards: Offshore oil development agreements signed with foreign oil companies covering disputed areas. "Since 1988, more than 30 production sharing contracts have been signed with foreign oil companies"  (Lien, "The Economics of Petroleum," 6.20). Between 1988 and 1994: “Vietnam Oil and Gas Corp., which reported directly to the prime minister, signed twenty-seven production-sharing agreements to allow foreign oil groups from dozens of countries to explore its offshore blocks.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 96). Practice of signing such agreements has continued to the present.
1989 January 14: VN holds awards ceremony for individuals and units involved in defending Spratlys (Zhang Liangfu NSQDDSJ, 178)

1989: PRC repeatedly criticises Vietnamese detentions of PRC fishers (Chen, "China's ASEAN policy," p.179). Implicitly this may have continued at least until 1994, when another similar case is identifiable.

1989 August: DK-1 rig building in Nam Con Son Basin commences. "In August 1989 Vietnam built facilities on Bombay Castle (on Rifleman Bank), Vanguard Bank, and Prince of Wales Bank, bringing to 24 the number of islets and reefs under its control." (Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, 22). August 19: China criticizes Vietnam's commencement of construction of an economic and scientific and technical service complex in the Truong Sa archipelago (Nansha, "Nanhai Zhudao"; VAFIS, "Sovereignty.").

1990, May 17: VN MOFA spokesman reads statement to the Mixed Committee of the UNESCO Oceanography Program saying China's Spratly scientific research activities are violating Vietnam's sovereignty & territorial integrity (Zhang Liangfu NSQDDSJ 190).
other_possible_cases: 1990-2000: Large increase in Vietnam’s fishing industry output thanks to various policies that promoted its development. Allows Vietnamese fishermen to increase presence in South China Sea. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 137). Would need to find more specific information for me to be comfortable including this, do avoid double counting, etc. (e.g. already including the Spratly Island fishing harbour, the aquatic products tax reduction, etc.) Agree. We have various cases of intensified VN fishing-related assertiveness in this decade and beyond

description: 1990 (onward): Vietnam significantly increases pace of drilling (wildcat wells), lasts at least through the 1990s (Lien, "The Economics of Petroleum," 6.12). According to a 1998 source, although offshore exploration drilling began in 1974, 78.4% of all wildcats were drilled after 1989. (Lien, "The Economics of Petroleum," 6.20).
1990: Vietnam builds DK-1 rig on Prince Consort Bank (Vuving, "South China Sea: Who Occupies What"). DK-1 rigs are classed as a demonstrative behavior, not use of force, since the area is underwater.
1991: Vietnam builds DK-1 platforms on Alexandra Bank and Grainger Bank (Vuving, "South China Sea: Who Occupies What"). AMTI confirms.

1992, June 27: Vietnamese state news agency reports Vietnam has built small fishing harbour on Spratly Island. (Zhang NSQDDSJ 230). PRC codemns in September 1994 (Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute 33; KYODO - 'China says Vietnam port encroaching on its waters').
other_possible_cases: 1992 July: Gaven Reef dispute. July (?): Official diplomatic protest was made with the MFA, reiterating Vietnamese sovty & accusing PRC of violating the Nov 1991 leaders' agreement. 1992-07-04: Chinese troops and building materials arrive at Gaven Reef 1992-07-04 Vietnam removes Chinese sovereignty marker on Gaven Reef. July 7: Vietnamese major state media report VN MOFA spokesperson making speech to reporters, criticizing China for setting up sovereignty marker on [Gaven Reef]. ("乐礁滩" (aka 加文礁) and "南阁文礁" (aka 南薰礁以南). A tugboat allegedly stopped to the north of 乐礁滩 and S of 南阁文礁 (10"10'N/114"15'E). July 9: China confirms military occupation of Gaven Reef. (南海诸岛大事年表) Probably not an act of assertiveness of Vietnam as reaction is milder than that in response to previous PRC actions.

description: 1992 May-June: Vietnam strongly protests Crestone's oil exploration, submitting a note to the United Nations (Hayton 2014). VN has regularly used UN channels to denounce PRC actions since; indeed this policy could be traced back as far as 1988.

1992, Sept 4: Vietnam summons PRC ambassador to protest and demand removal of a survey ship and drilling ship from Gulf of Tonkin. Reuters describes this as the toughest statement against Chinese actions since February. (Zhang NSQDDSJ, 233) On September 5: “Hanoi even warned Beijing of the possibility of using force to ward off two Chinese vessels exploring for oil in the Gulf of Tonkin.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea 80).
1992 October 18: Vietnam sends meterological and resource survey team to Spratlys (Zhang NSQDDSJ 235)

1992: Increased tempo and expanded geographical scope of oil and gas agreements with foreign companies. Jan 30 1992: "Arabian Oil Co. of Japan and Taikoku Oil Co. reached an agreement with Vietnam to explore oil and gas reserves off the country's southern shore. The area in question is a 2,500 square kilometer area in the South China Sea, 350 km southeast of Vung Tau. The agreement is the first for a Japanese company in Vietnamese territory where reserves at estimated at 1.5 to 3 billion barrels" (Taffer dataset). In 1992 Vietnam also signed contracts with Indonesia's Astra Petronusa, and in April of 1992 signed a joint development agreement with Malaysia. (Taffer dataset). Zhang lists the latter as occuring in January (Zhang, "Appendix II"). In June, Vietnam signed oil contracts with Norwegian company NOPEC.  This area overlaps with WAB-21. (Zhang, "Appendix II")

1993 March onwards: Vietnam takes a series of measures retaliating against PRC moves over WAB-21 and Gulf of Tonkin. Vietnam approves Mobil involvement in "Blue Dragon" development and in December 1993 explore in Block 5.1b within the 9DL, near Crestone concession, though not overlapping (Nansha, "Nanhai Zhudao"; Fravel 2008, 297; Hayton 2014). Crestone's Thompson was invited to Hanoi for meeting with PetroVietnam, who offers him joint venture in return for cancelling CNOOC deal. Thompson declined (Hayton 2014). A month after accusing PRC of resuming oil exploration in the Gulf of Tonkin in September 1993, Vietnam invited oil companies to bid on nine offshore blocks, including contract areas around Vanguard Bank and Prince of Wales Bank within the PRC WAB-21 block. "On 19 April Mobil signed a production-sharing contract with PetroVietnam for Block 5-1b (Blue Dragon)." And "north of the Crestone area, PetroVietnam and Nopec offered offshore licenses in Vietnamese blocks 122-130." (Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, 28-30). This offering by PetroVietnam was reported on November 12: ""Nine tracts are involved, designated blocks 122-130 and covering more than 60,000 sq km extending from southeastern waters to the central part of the South China Sea which Hanoi prefers to call its Eastern Sea. To ensure interest from foreign oil companies, Petrovietnam is sweetening its production sharing terms and, for the first time, staging "road shows", or promotional seminars. The offshore tracts opened for tender are described as "frontier" and are largely unexplored, mainly because they lie in deeper waters and in the disputed area claimed by China. However, Nopec international marketing and business development manager Halfdan Castens says the lower blocks may have potential for oil and the northern part may be gas-prone. However, an executive of a British oil firm operating in the country doubted Vietnam would be successful in luring western oil firms into the troubled and deep waters. According to Nopec, water depths range from near-shore to more than 2,000 metres. Nopec's Castens stressed not all blocks were in disputed waters." (International Gas Report, via Taffer dataset)
other_possible_cases: 1993 April: Vietnam Continental Shelf Committee deputy chief publishes paper in national defense magazine titled "Combining the Resolution of Maritime Boundary Disputes and the Management of the Oceans" (VIETNAM IMPLIES SPRATLYS & PARACELS GENERATE NO EEZ RIGHTS; Zhang NSQDDSJ 244)

description: 1993 April: Vietnam sending civilian immigrants to Spratlys, according to Vietnamese media interview with D/PM 陈德良 who recently inspected there. The D/PM was quoted by Vietnam's military paper (via Xinhua, via Yomiuri Shimbun) as stating, "On these [five] islands there is already an immigration program . . . in order to unify economic tasks and national defense objectives, [we] must strengthen economic activities and civilian activities." (Zhang NSQDDSJ 246). According to one PRC source, Vietnamese immigration to Spratlys began in late 1980s, encouraged by preferential policies such as low- or no-interest loans to buy boats, and the development of infrastructure such as schools (Zhang NSQDDSJ 257-9).

1993 Aug 7: "On 7 August Vietnam provided an export tax exemption for fishing in the Spratly islands." Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, 28). On June 4, 1994 Vietnamese authorities make Spratly aquatic products tax-free (Nansha, "Nanhai Zhudao").
1993 Nov: New Vietnam lighthouse on Southwest Cay (Nanzi). (Zhang, NSQDDSJ 265; Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, 29).

1993, early: Expanded scope of oil and gas drilling, moving further offshore. On Feb 27 SCMP reports that BP "has confirmed hitting "extremely high-pressure" natural gas at the Lan Tay-1 exploration well, and is currently dealing with a blow-out, or uncontrolled flow of gas, near the well, 430 kilometres southeast of Ho Chi Minh City...Reliable oil industry officials in Singapore and Vietnam say BP has struck high-pressure gas within a very thick subterranean formation at the Lan Do-1 well site. "It could be very big," said one oil-man. Both wells are located in Block 06, where BP is drilling in partnership with Oil and Natural Gas Commission-Videsh of India and Statoil, the Norwegian state oil company, under licence from the Vietnam Government." (SCMP via Taffer dataset).

1994 May-June - June 1995: Lighthouse-building project expands  in Spratly Islands. Vietnam builds 42m lighthouse on Ladd Reef, and 22m lighthouse on West Reef, 30nm from Ladd Reef (Nansha, "Nanhai Zhudao"; Zhang, "Appendix II").
other_possible_cases: April-May: Strong statements in Vietnamese media and from MOFA officials over Crestone & WAB-21 (Hayton)

description: 1994 April-August: Vietnam escalates in response to Crestone tensions. In April a naval incident involves a Chinese vessel carrying out seismic research for Crestone and Vietnamese vessels ordering it to quit an area considered by them to be under Vietnamese jurisdiction. The Chinese vessel may have followed the order. (FEER October 13, 1994, quoted in VAFIS, "Sovereignty").  "During May or June 1994 PetroVietnam began to drill in Vietnam’s block 135, which is within Crestone’s concession from the PRC." (Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Dispute, 28-30). Rig is VietSovPetro's Tam Sao, and the move prompts a two-month standoff with PRC ships (Hayton). In August armed vessels from Vietnam confront Crestone & Chinese company's collaborative drilling in Van An Bac (Blocks 133-135) (Vietnam.vn, "Chronicle of major events")
other_possible_cases: May: PetroVietnam moves VietSovPetro drilling rig Tam Dao into Block 135, within WAB-21 on the Vanguard Bank. PRC sends two ships to block supplies and a two-month standoff ensues. (Hayton)

description: 1994,  July 8: Vietnam 9th National Congress 5th Session passes UNCLOS motion claiming Paracels and Spratlys.PRC MFA spokesperson Shen Guofang denounces, says China is ready to shelve disputes and jointly develop. (RMRB p. 4 外交部发言人举行记者招待会 重申中国对西沙和南沙群岛的立场) National assembly had authorized ratification of UNCLOS on June 23. (Vietnam circulates report on UNCLOS implementation; Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 75).

1994 July 2: Vietnam seized three Chinese fishing boats and detained their crews (Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, 31). China protested [stern representations] the Vietnam's seizure and demanded the return of the vessels and the crew.  (MID 3.0 narratives #4030) Was in Gulf of Tonkin acc. MFA spokes Shen Guofang (Zhang Liangfu NSQDDSJ, 265) Sources in Taffer dataset concur.

1994, late: Vietnam started oil production in two more fields, Dai Hung (Big Bear) (Block 05– 1) and also at the ostensibly undisputed Rong (Dragon) (Block 16). (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 96).

1995, early: Vietnamese construction follows the PRC occupation of Mischief Reef.  "On 28 February Vietnam announced that it had reinforced its Spratly outposts." (Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, 37; see also Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 84-85).
diminished_notes: 1995, Dec 1: Le reportedly (according to AP) says he supports Philippines' Congress Speaker's proposal to "symbolically" reduce military forces posted in the Spratlys (Zhang Liangfu NSQDDSJ 290)

description: 1995, June: Lighthouse-building expands into Malaysian claimed area as Vietnam also "inaugurated" a new lighthouse on Amboyna Cay in June 1995. (Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, 38).

1995, May 26: Expansion of fishing in Spratlys. Japanese media report that "Provincial authorities in Vietnam have sent fishing trawlers to the disputed Spratly Islands in the South China Sea for a fishing and exploration mission. The maritime service in Ninh Thuan Province said it had sent two boats to the archipelago and if the first mission was successful more vessels would be sent later. Last week authorities in the neighbouring province of Khanh Hoa sent a fleet of 22 trawlers to the Spratlys." (Japan Economic Newswire via Taffer dataset)

1996 April: Energy development agreements with third-country oil companies in new areas. "Vietnam asserted its UNCLOS rights, authorising a consortium led by Conoco Vietnam Exploration and Production BV, a unit of Houstonbased Conoco Inc., to explore Blocks 133 and 134, which encompassed three million acres of the South Con Son basin, about 200 miles off Vietnam’s southern coast. These offshore acreages were also situated within Tu Chinh area (Vanguard Bank) that overlapped with the northwestern part of the South China Sea area China National Offshore Oil Corporation (CNOOC) and Crestone referred to as Wan’an Bei-21 (WAB-21; see Figure 2.10). As compared with its production-sharing agreement with Mobil Oil in 1994, Hanoi’s Conoco enterprise made an even deeper inroad into the WAB-21 area that China claimed.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 95; Dzurek, The Spratly Islands Disupute, 42).
diminished_notes: 1996 June (ish): Vietnam tones down its protests against China’s baselines law before Li Peng’s visit to Hanoi. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 99)

description: 1997 March: First use of ASEAN to push back against PRC, following the PRC's Kantan-03 oil rig move. On March 20 "in an unprecedented move, Vietnam’s Deputy Foreign Minister Vu Khoan met with the ambassadors of seven ASEAN members to inform them of the oil-drilling dispute and explain Vietnam’s position. The day after, Hanoi held a press conference to condemn China’s violation of its EEZ and continental shelf.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 99).

1998 January: “Vietnamese soldiers fire on a Philippine fishing boat near Vietnam-controlled Tennent (Pigeon) Reef, injuring a Filipino fisherman.” (Van Pham, The Use or Threat of Force in the South China Sea Disputes, 527; "Philippines Lodges Protest Over Shooting in Spratlys," Deutsche Presse-Agentur, January 19, 1998)
other_possible_cases: 1998: Vietnam occupies 2 additional features (Fravel 2008 p298). Didn't see this anywhere else. Agree, this may be a slip - he might be referring to the Philippines and Malaysia, or the Ba Ke Reef construction

description: 1998 July-August: New DK-1 platforms at Orleana (Aonan) and Kingston (Jindun) Shoals (Chen Qi, "Expansion and Military Deployment; Fravel, Strong Borders, 298); Vietnam constructs “two economic-scientific technological service stations in the Spratly Islands (Ba Ke reefs)"; China protests. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 101).
other_possible_cases: 1998: Law of the Sea of Vietnam first proposed, but enactment delayed until 2012. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 200-1). Not a case of intensified assertiveness as they didn't actually do it.

description: 1999 October: Vietnamese forces allegedly fire warning shots at Philippine aircraft flying over Vietnam-controlled areas of the Spratly Islands. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 101; Van Pham, The Use or Threat of Force in the South China Sea Disputes, 528; "RP Protests Viets Firing at Place," Manila Standard)

1999: In ASEAN preparations for drafts for a code of conduct in the South China Sea, Vietnam advocates for the Paracel Islands to be included in the Code, which some other ASEAN parties disagreed with. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 111). Continues pushing for this until Declaration of Conduct in 2002. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 116; (Storey 'Trouble and strife…')
other_possible_cases: 1999: China imposes first unilateral fishing ban in the South China Sea, Vietnam protests. Vietnam protesting is nothign new, but the ban is, so..? (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 101) Agree, protest is not new.

description: 2000: Lighthouse construction at Pigeon Reef (Tiên Nữ / Tennant Reef) (Zhang, "Appendix II")

2001: "China reacted angrily when Vietnam set up a local government in the Spratlys similar to other administrative districts in the country." (Vietnam celebrates claim to Spratley islands). "on February 10 [Vietnam] claimed to establish a "local government" in the Spratly Islands to "facilitate administration", "never give up an inch of land", and "will not hesitate to fight." (Sina via Taffer dataset).

2001: Intensified detentions of PRC fishers in Spratlys. "Chinese fisherman Lin Guanyong knows he has a perilous job working in the South China Sea, and it is not just the weather. He was detained once by the Vietnamese authorities in 2001, after he and his 20 crewmates were arrested and charged with illegal fishing in Vietnam's waters. Their boat was towed to a port in Vietnam, where they stayed on board, while another boat was sent back to China to get the US$2,500 (S$3,400) needed to pay their fine. They were released after two weeks." (Straits Times via Taffer dataset). "May 2 2001 (AFP) - A Chinese fishing boat with 11 crew aboard was seized by two Vietnamese warships in the South China Sea a week ago and has not been heard of since, a Hong Kong newspaper reported Wednesday." The fishing vessel was named as Danzhou 72007 (AFP via Taffer dataset). And as reported on June 13: "Coastguards in central Vietnam have seized four Chinese boats and 51 crew members caught fishing in Vietnamese waters, a local official said on Wednesday. The official from the People's Committee in Thua Thien Hue province said the four boats were seized on Sunday. He said he expected the fisherman would soon be released but they would first be required to provide written confirmation of their violation and pay some fines." (Reuters via Taffer dataset). This occurred in the Spratlys at least back to 2001, and probably earlier: "Returning back to the Spratlys, Cheng writes that other countries are increasing the areas they are patrolling from their occupied features, reducing the area available for Chinese fishing. Qionghai 03688 琼·琼海03688 captain Wang Weimin 王维民 shows the journalist a gunshot scar inflicted by Vietnamese soldiers over a decade ago. That time, Wang said, one of his boatmates was beaten to death." (Chubb, "Adventure, regret, anger"). PRC internal and public sources report numbers of PRC boats subject to coercion in the Spratlys by Vietnam among others in 2006 and 2008-09 (NISCSS, Nanhai Xingshi 2006 and 2008-09; Chubb, "Relax, wife"). PRC media reports continued to report instances of VN coercion against PRC fishers in Spratlys as late as mid-2012 (Chubb, "A certain neighbouring country").

2002 August: “Vietnamese troops fire warning shots at Philippine military reconnaissance planes circling over Spratlys.” (Van Pham, The Use or Threat of Force in the South China Sea Disputes, 529; Tran Dinh Thanh Lam, "Bird Watchers, Divers, Tourists Ignite Spratlys Row,” Asia Times Online).
other_possible_cases: 2002 June: Reported that Vietnam’s coast guard arrested 9 Chinese fishing vessels and 179 crew members for fishing (illegally) in the Vietnamese side of the Gulf of Tonkin. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 107). Not an act of assertiveness if it was on the VN side, ie. not in the disputed area.

description: 2003, April-June: When China sent a scientific research ship to the Spratlys, "Vietnamese navy sent ships to constantly monitor it, impeding China's normal scientific research activities" (NISCSS 2003 report, 36). Internal PRC source.
other_possible_cases: 2003, September 23: Vietnam arrests Chinese fishers in Gulf of Tonkin on Sept 23, detains them in haiphong, releases on Sept 27. (The foreign vessels for infringement…). Happened year before, so this instance probably should just be shown as continuity? Ye - and not assertive if it wasn't in the disputed area.

description: 2003, November: "In November Hanoi formally warned Taipei to stop violating its sovereignty by driving away Vietnamese fishing boats near the disputed South China Sea archipelago." (Vietnam condemns Taiwan…). In March 2004 Vietnam strongly protests Taiwanese construction at Ban Than Reef in the Spratly Islands. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 126; Vietnam condemns Taiwan over Spratlys construction). Verbal assertiveness against ROC appears to have diminished or disappeared after that.

2004 April: Spratly tourism commences. Vietnam “announced a controversial plan to open a boat tour for civilians to one of the Spratly Islands, which it described as ‘normal civilian activity.’” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 126). First tour on April 19 with 100 tourists. (SOA Memo 2004; China irks…; China indignant…; Zhang, "Appendix II") Boat tours have continued to the present.

2004 onward: Depletion of fish stocks in Vietnam’s coastal areas and China-Vietnam Gulf of Tonkin fisheries agreement pushes Vietnamese fishermen further out into the South China Sea. Increased presence of Vietnamese fishing vessels in Paracel Islands, resulting in more incidents with Chinese fishery administration vessels. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 137).
other_possible_cases: 2004: Vietnam begins modernizing Spratly Island runway (CSIS 2017, 237). Airstrip already exists and counted as assertive, so including this upgrade would probably be double coutning. Unless it made a difference to VN's local military capabilities

description: 2004: Infrastructure upgrades in Spratlys.  Vietnam begins modernizing Spratly Island runway (CSIS 2017, 237), and on May 29 Vietnam Posts and Telecommunications Corporation announces it will use a satellite link to provide Internet service to soldiers in the Spratlys. (Internet to play role in islands spat)
other_possible_cases: 2004 March: Vietnam strongly protests Taiwanese construction at Ban Than Reef in the Spratly Islands. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 126; Vietnam condemns Taiwan over Spratlys construction). Seems stronger than usual, maybe? count this?

description: 2004 September: PetroVietnam offers nine offshore blocks to international oil firms in the Phu Khanh Basin in the central/south part. “It should be noted that almost all previous offerings were in the Song Hong Basin in the north and Cuu Long Basin and Nam Con Son Basin in the south.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 136; Vietnam rejects China's Spratly oil…; NISCSS 2004 report p.13) Signing of PSCs over these blocks (122-128) would become targets of PRC coercion from 2006 (KNOC, "Vietnam Acreage")

2006 June-July: Chinese survey ships carrying out seismic work south of the Paracels allegedly "fended off waves of Vietnamese “armed vessels” (武装船) sent to obstruct the survey." (Martinson, The Arming of China's Maritime Frontier, 7-8). Happened in June 2007 as well as 2010 and 2014, so arguably an ongoing line of behavior through that period.
other_possible_cases: 2005 January: [in context of China pressuring Vietnam after Vietnam sells oil blocks] Chinese maritime policy open fire killing 9 Vietnamese fishermen, and Vietnam’s foreign ministry “went public to criticize China in an unusually strong language for killing and injuring honest Vietnamese fishermen who were legally fishing in the western side of the Gulf of Tonkin.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 138-9; CABLE #05HANOI247) PRC action was of unprecedented severity, so hard to say it was an intensification

description: 2006, June 16: India's ONGC Videsh signs up for Blocks 127 and 128. "In 2006, ONGC Videsh, an Indian state-owned oil exploration corporation, obtained permission from Vietnam to explore several blocks (including 127 and 128) in the South China Sea in waters also claimed by China" (ICG, Oil in Troubled Waters, 12, KNOC, Vietnam Acreage Map). This broadened the disputed area covered by contracts with third-country oil companies.
2007: Continental Shelf surveys ahead of UNCLOS deadline, which continue through 2008 (Wikileaks cables). Only China appears to have objected.
diminished_notes: 2007 April – September: Reported that 5 Vietnamese energy projects with foreign partners are suspended in face of Chinese pressure. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 140). ( For more specifics see: Hayton; Reilly 2012; SCS incidents file; va
other_possible_cases: 2007 February 9: Vietnam adopts Resolution 09—NQ/TW (“Maritime Strategy Toward 2020”). Not quite sure why this was in the cases - how was It new assertiveness?

description: 2007, April: Vietnam elevates Truong Sa (Spratly Island) to the level of a “township” under the Truong Sa District. (Swaine & Fravel, "China's Assertive Behavior," pp.15-16)

2007 August 6: “Vietnam officially demanded the US ocean drilling company, Transocean, to cancel its concession agreement with CNOOC for Block 2-4 west of the Paracel Islands, which overlapped with Vietnam’s Block 141.” [response to oil tensions] (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 141). Also: “Since 2007, Vietnamese officials repeatedly asked their US counterparts to pay more attention to the East Asia and particularly to dissuade the US companies from dropping their projects in the waters offshore Vietnam.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 182).
2007 December: Vietnam’s first ever public demonstrations about the South China Sea. (Hayton, The South China Sea, 151, 153). Subsequent cases were seen in 2008, 2011 and 2014.

2008, January: "China accused Vietnamese fishermen of attacking Chinese trawlers in the Gulf of Tonkin. Vietnam responded that Vietnamese and Chinese fishing boats had merely bumped into each other after getting their nets entangled." (Storey 'Trouble and strife…'). Jan 17 2008: "China has asked Vietnam to seriously investigate a recent robbery of some of its fishing vessels by Vietnamese fishermen in the Beibu Gulf. "China is highly concerned about the case, and has made representations to Vietnam and required the Vietnamese side to seriously investigate and handle the case, and at the same time, take effective measures to avoid further cases," said Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Jiang Yu at a regular press conference here on Thursday." (Xinhua via Taffer database).
other_possible_cases: 2008, September: Vietnam protests (not formal protest) Chinese netizens' claims of a plan to invade over the SCS ('080911 - China's netizens menace Vietnam'), ('Having fun at Vietnam's expense'). Also sthere are street protests. Covered under 2007 case.

description: 2008, July: Vietnam signs preliminary cooperation agreement with US company Exxon Mobil to explore disputed areas in the southern and central coastal areas. (NISCSS 2009 report p.11). 2008, early: Exxon signs MOU with PetroVietnam to explore Blocks 156-159. "The blocks were by far the furthest offshore that Vietnam had ever leased. The south-eastern corner of Block 159 was more than 500km from the Vietnamese coast – well into disputed territory. ExxonMobil was also in serious talks about leasing Blocks 117, 118 and 119 just off Vietnam’s central coast." (Hayton 2014)

2008: Vietnam's diplomatic lobbying efforts stepped up. Vietnamese opposition forced a Swiss offshore drilling company to cancel a Paracels contract with China (CSIS 2017, 204). Also in 2008 Vietnam managed to lobby IOC to remove China's 9-dash-line in the official online map of the Olympic torch relay (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 157).

2008: Vietnam's domestic public opinion campaign stepped up. The Vietnamese government urges mass media and press to launch propaganda to raise public awareness of Vietnam’s sovereignty over Paracels and Spratlys. “We must assert absolute sovereignty over the country’s land and waters to maintain stability and peace for growth,” noted President Nguyen Minh Triet, who had a working session this week with the army forces of Military Zone No5, the patrol unit of sea and waters including Hoang Sa and Truong Sa." (Vietnam News Brief Service via Taffer dataset). Late 2008 saw further “Major changes in Vietnam’s information policy in the maritime domain...New instructions from CPV’s Central Commission for Publicity and Education on 2008 November 26, followed by a succession of state-funded nation-wide propaganda campaigns, a propaganda conference on the SCS in March 2009 in Hai Phong. Much more media coverage and critical public discussion followed. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 158-160).

2008 (late) onward: In addition to domestic information policy changes, Vietnam also steps up more international outreach to advance its position such as Track II workshops, and protests by Vietnamese scholars against inclusion of 9-dash-line in various publications (e.g. Google Maps, National Geographic, Science) (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 160-163; also "Swaine & Fravel, China's Assertive Behavior," 16).

2009, early April: Vietnam gives 21 families living in the Spratlys a deposit book with 5 million dong, and officially commissions Chairman of Hoang Sa County People’s Committee. (NISCSS 2009 report, p.12).

2009 May 6 and 7: Vietnam presents joint submission with Malaysia on its southern continental shelf to the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf, and a partial report on its northern continental coast. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 171).

2009 May (onward): Vietnam intensifies opposition to China’s extended unilateral fishing ban. The Vietnam Fishery Association continues to encourage fishermen to sail off with the purpose of “both doing business as usual and asserting Vietnam’s sovereignty and jurisdiction,” and “When the fishing boats were captured, Hanoi issued protests through the statement of the MOFA spokespersons and diplomatic notes, and worked through bilateral channels with Chinese authorities to secure their release.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 174-5)

2009, Sept 21-22: Vietnamese ships "shadow and harrass" USNS Victorious in SCS. (WIKILEAKS #09HANOI895) Location unknown, but perhaps most likely to have occurred around Vietnam's straight baselines encompassing Con Son Island, as Vietnam's "excessive straight baselines" are noted as a target in the DoD's 2009-2010 FONOP report.

2009 onwards: Land reclamation and other infrastructure upgrades in the Spratlys. Starts with lighthouses at Sand Cay and Spratly Island (Zhang, "Appendix II") but also extended tp communications and defence infrastructure: "From 2009 to 2014, radar and communications equipment were added at 15 outposts, quality-of-life improvements at 19, point defenses at 18, new helipads at 6, and civilian infrastructure improvements at 5 outposts. By 2016, Vietnam had created 120 acres of new land at 10 different features in the Spratlys. This includes Cornwallis South Reef, which had been fully submerged and is beyond Vietnam’s continental shelf claim." US Department of Defense referred to VN “the most active claimant in terms of both outpost upgrades and land reclamation” prior to China’s island building campaign (CSIS 2017, 237).

2010: Vietnam pushes South China Sea internationalization via its occupation of the rotating ASEAN Chair, facilitating US statement of national interest in the South China Sea, and criticism of PRC's recent actions. Wanted to push for a legally binding code of conduct, and the ASEAN Foreign Ministers Meeting joint statement in July had stronger language on South China Sea. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 179-186).
other_possible_cases: 2010: VN ships "surrounded a Chinese Fisheries Law Enforcement Command ship patrolling disputed waters and also confronted a Chinese survey team 100 miles east of Vietnam’s Ly Son Island" (CSIS 2017, 204). Somewhat debatable case - PRC FLEC activities increased, so VN's response may have been implicit at earlier times,  and the PRC survey might have been in a new area, and thus this kind of VN response to such PRC behaviour was implicit from the 2006 and 2007 confrontations onwards.

description: 2010,  April 1 State President of Vietnam Nguyen Minh Triet visited Bach Long Vi in the Gulf of Tonkin to make a strong proclamation (“will not give up an inch of our motherland”). (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 179; https://tuoitre.vn/khong-de-bat-cu-ai-xam-lan-bo-coi-371469.htm).

2011 May-June: Binh Minh 02 incident(s). May: Vietnamese Ministry of Foreign Affairs holds a press conference specifically to condemn and show footage of Chinese vessels cutting the exploration cable of a Vietnamese survey ship, the Binh Minh 02. This was an escalated response in terms of publicity [Vietnam preferred to deal with these things privately for the past decade]. Similar incident two weeks later (and similarly public response from Vietnam). June: Strong statements from Vietnamese leaders after 2nd incident. Defense minister raises issue at Shrangri-La Dialogue. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 187-8; Thayer 'China's new wave...')

2011: June: Several consecutive weeks of anti-China protests allowed in Hanoi, escalating the struggle in the domestic public opinion field. Tamping down in Hanoi reportedly began in early July, but attracted anger on the internet, leading to permission of further controlled protests (TODAY & AFP, via Taffer dataset).

2011, June 13: Vietnam holds "routine" live-fire drill for six hours around Hon Ong Island about 40 kilometres off Quang Nam province, 250 kilometres away from the Paracels, 1000km from Spratlys. (Raman - Eurasia Review) “Reportedly, the exercise lasted for nine hours and involved in coastal artillery and corvette-based missiles.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 188)

2011 onward: Vietnam reclamation and infrastructure upgrades in the Spratlys stepped up again. Reclamation begins at Pearson Reef in 2011, and Sand Cay upgrades begin the same year (Zhang, "Appendix II"). 2011, May 26: PH media reports "A Philippine government briefing paper said that “Vietnam is at the forefront of construction activities, having built the most number of additional structures at its occupied territories since 1998.”  -- mainly solar panels, buildings, piers, sea walls, gun emplacements ('Vietnam beefs up..) West Reef, Central Reef and Grierson Reef follow in 2012 (Zhang, "Appendix II"). In total "five acres [added] at Sand Cay and 16 acres at West Reef. New facilities and defensive structures were also added. These reportedly included artillery and shoulder-fired anti- aircraft missiles." (CSIS 2017, 237).
2012 May: Two maritime militia platoons set up in Vietnam in Khan Hoa. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 179).
other_possible_cases: 2012 May: Vietnam sends note protesting China’s inclusion of 9-dash-line on Chinese passports. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 200). Not new, but the passports were new. Probably not worth including. Yes, appears a routine response to a new situation.

description: 2012 June: Vietnam National Assembly passes Law of the Sea of Vietnam, first proposed in 1998. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 172, 200).
other_possible_cases: 2012 December (7?): Public protest in Vietnam after Chinese ships cut the seismic cables of the Binh Minh 02 for the second time, and a month after China rolled out its passports including the 9-dash line. About 200 people show up. Vietnamese law enforcement shuts down the protest. (Hayton, The South China Sea, 151-3, 6). Again not sure how to count, since it is not state sanctioned activity but still important. This is actually a diminishment of assertiveness, compared with how VN reacted in 2011 to the pair of similar incidents in May-June.

description: 2013 January: Vietnam “implicitly supported the Philippines’ legal proceeding… Deputy Chairman of Vietnam Foreign Ministry’s National Border Committee said that countries have the right to settle the disputes in conformity with the UN Charter and international law.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 206).

2013, July: Spratly flight activity intensifies. "More than four years ago, on July 3, 2013, after reassigning the Air Force Regiment 954 to be under the direction of the Navy, the Naval Air Force Brigade 954 has been equipped with a variety of new, modern aircraft for the implementation of training on anti-submarine, aerial reconnaissance, transporting to Truong Sa and DK1 oil rigs, and search and rescue work....Since 2013, Squadron 2 alone conducted over 4,000 flights, including more than 300 training flights and other passenger missions to visit Truong Sa, as well as many search and rescue flights and flights transporting goods to serve the army and people on the islands." (Flights bring Truong Sa closer to the mainland - Nhan Dan Online)

2014 May-July: HYSY 981 crisis. VN maritime law enforcement ships and maritime militia battle fiercely to try to disrupt PRC oil drilling operation close to Triton Island in the Paracels. PRC accuses Vietnam of ramming its ships "a total of 1416 times".

2014, May-July: Vietnam mounts unprecedented international public opinion campaign. Foreign journalists are brought along on Vietnamese maritime law enforcement ships as it deploys coast guard to confront Chinese oil rig HYSY 981 and accompanying vessels. Vietnamese officials and many levels call for talks but are rejected. Vietnamese leaders also threaten legal action and raise the issue with partners, in multilateral settings, and so on. Paints China as bully through series of press conferences. (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 202-3; Hayton 2014, 158).

2014 December 5: Vietnam lodges Statement of Interest to PCA over Philippines' SCS arbitration. “After two years of consideration, on 5 December 2014, Hanoi decided to undertake the third option, lodging a Statement of Interest to ask the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) between the Philippines and China in The Hague to take due regard of its opinions, rights and interests. Vietnam’s Statement of Interest recognises the PCA’s jurisdiction over the Philippine’s case, restates Vietnam’s claim to sovereignty over the Spratlys and Paracels, refutes China’s nine-dash line claim, and reserves the right to seek to intervene appropriately if necessary.” (Do Thanh Hai, Vietnam and the South China Sea, 207). More broadly, Vietnamese leaders such as PM Nguyen Tan Dung began discussing the possibility of following the Philippines into legal channels against China over the SCS.

2015: Stepped-up land reclamation in the Spratlys, particularly at Spratly Island, where 37 acres were added between 2014 and early 2016, enabling a runway extension completed the following year, and West Reef, where 70 acres were added between 2013 and early 2016 (AMTI, "Vietnam's Island Building"). Other locations include Collins, Discovery Great, Barque Canada (Zhang, "Appendix II").
other_possible_cases: 2015, June: New luxury tourist cruise to Spratlys offered, as well as possible civilian flights. Not clear if the tour constituted an escalation, and planned civilian flights seem not to have gone ahead. (Reuters, "Vietnam launches special 'sovereignty' cruise, likely to irk China")
